items.body:
Over the course of the last decade, the group أحمد [Ahmed] has carved out a distinctive approach to the jazz canon through their tireless exploration of the music of Ahmed Abdul-Malik. Mining Abdul-Malik’s compositions and his incorporation of non-Western microtonality into the jazz vocabulary, pianist Pat Thomas, alto saxophone player Seymour Wright, bassist Joel Grip, and drummer Antonin Gerbal have done more than reinterpretation. They have used the music as a foundation for both immersion and subversion of the way that the standard jazz quartet functions within post-bop structures. For last year’s Sama'a (Audition), they went into the studio for an expansive refraction of Abdul-Malik’s Jazz Sahara. During that same session, the four took a slight detour to record Play Monk, a dive into deconstructions of six pieces by Thelonious Monk, all but one of which he recorded in the late 1950s when Abdul-Malik was part of his group. أحمد [Ahmed] has incorporated Monk tunes into their live sets but this is the first time they have focused on his tunes on a recording.

While Thomas, Wright, Grip, and Gerbal have not altered their strategies in the switch of source material, there is one significant shift in the way one listens to this music. A quick search returns no other versions of Abdul-Malik’s pieces other than those recorded by the composer or أحمد [Ahmed] whereas Monk’s “Epistrophy” or “’Round Midnight” have hundreds. Even a less well-known piece like “Oska T” has dozens. Because the pieces covered are so well known, their teasing apart and restructuring of the underlying thematic kernels are more readily evident. Over two CDs, the quartet digs in, with improvisations that range between 20 and 30 minutes with the exception of a seven-minute extrapolation of “Epistrophy.” These extended explorations allow the group to excavate the forms with a focused patience, zeroing in on and elucidating microscopic details, extricating them into the fundamental elements of penetrating improvisations.

The first phrases of the opening “Bye-ya / Epistrophy” provide a glimpse of what is to come. Bass and piano circle around the theme and Gerbal’s lithe drumming circles up to drive momentum. Wright’s stabbing alto picks apart the melody and the four launch off on a circuitous inquiry, dismantling Monk’s tune into its constituent fragments and then reassembling them with constructivist abstraction. Each of the four seize on elements of the underlying piece, playing them off of each other with unwavering resolve, an approach the group continues to advance in their sweeping live sets. There is an insistent intensity as Wright’s notes pick and prod at Thomas’ skewed clusters, Grip’s free walking lines, and Gerbal’s churning free rhythms. Shards of “Epistrophy” are introduced into the mix by Grip and Thomas, slowly accruing with multifaceted erudition.

The group continues to subvert expectations with “Friday the Thirteenth” as Thomas insistently repeats the first phrase of the tune against Grip’s growling arco inversions. Wright’s keypad pops and Gerbal’s open percussion build momentum and Wright unleashes spattered honks that open into a collective four-part splintering of the theme, picking it apart and recasting it with angular exactitude, building density and intensity over the course of the sweeping 26-minute improvisation. “’Round Midnight” gets a relatively straightforward introduction with Wright intoning the theme over sinuous bass and cymbal splashes. Thomas’ spare chords enter as the quartet dynamically transposes the constituent parts of the piece with imperturbable resolution resolving with the riveting cycling hushed snare abrasions that brings the piece to a close.

A seven-minute scorching, stuttering run through “Epistrophy” serves as an interlude to an abstracted, cascading reading of “Evidence” which takes Monk’s stop-start theme and explodes it with relentless, spiraled piano phrases and the hurtling momentum of bass and drums driving Wright’s coruscating alto which prods and jabs with spiky dexterity. The 30-minute improvisation is an engulfing exemplification of unflagging invention. Monk’s “Oska T.,” structured around an obsessively cyclical riff, is a fitting conclusion to the release. The quartet slows things down to a free shuffle with bass and alto arcing over the mutable pulse of piano and drums. The four players adroitly weave their lines in and out of the collective undercurrent with indefatigable ingenuity. While others have dedicated themselves to the reinterpretation of the music of Thelonious Monk, أحمد [Ahmed]’s Play Monk is distinctive in its mastery, fully absorbing his music into the collective rigor and artistry of this singular ensemble.

items._cn_summary: 这张双CD专辑由四位欧洲即兴乐手组成的团体录制，他们此前一直致力于重新发掘爵士贝斯手Ahmed Abdul-Malik的作品，此次则将视线转向Thelonious Monk的六首曲目——这些作品大多录制于Abdul-Malik作为Monik乐队成员时的1950年代末。与演绎Abdul-Malik冷门作品不同，Monk的曲目如《Epistrophy》和《'Round Midnight》拥有大量录音版本，因此乐团的拆解与重构更为显眼。六首作品以二十分钟至三十分钟的时长展开（仅《Epistrophy》演绎为七分钟），通过极度耐心和聚焦的方式挖掘形式内部的微观细节。钢琴手Pat Thomas的偏斜音簇、 alto萨克斯手Seymour Wright的穿刺式音符、贝斯手Joel Grip的自由行走线条与鼓手Antonin Gerbal的搅动节奏相互碰撞，将Monk的旋律碎片拆解后以构成主义式的抽象重新组合，展现出对后波普结构的沉浸式颠覆。

items.body: It usually takes me some time to adjust to the pace of Cristián Alvear’s guitar playing, but by the time I get there I don’t want to leave. From Michael Pisaro’s ‘melody, silence’, through works by Radu Malfatti and Ryoko Akama, to this two-disc collection of music by Jürg Frey, the Chilean has recorded some of the sparsest, sparest music I’ve heard. Across “guitarist, alone”, single notes drop like pebbles into a pool of silence, the ripples dispersing and disappearing before the next sound is heard. In the wrong mood, listening can be tedious. It can also be like a slow-acting spirit, its warmth gradually seeping into my bones and spreading through my body. To understand Frey’s music solely in terms of silence and its opposite would be to do the Swiss composer a disservice: “guitarist, alone” is rife with rumours of melody and traces of song. Occasionally, echoes of previous guitar musics — Baroque, Spanish classical guitar — can be faintly heard in the slip of a cadence or the fading of a note, like wandering through an empty house from room to room, sometimes perceiving the barest marks of previous inhabitance. Or like discerning in the gentle rise and fall of a landscape the shape of a cairn. A run of notes can sound like a melodic figure or abstract, isolated tones, depending on how you hear it; repeated listens trample down the grass into a path, or wear away the surface of a certainty until it vanishes. Alvear’s disciplined and focused playing allows this change to occur, allowing neither figure nor abstraction, nor a polarisation of the two, to become set in stone. The first disc of the release is given over to ‘50 Sächelchen’ (‘50 Little things’) from 1989, and this half-century of short pieces demonstrates a wide range of styles, from arching melodies to falling patterns to long held notes to moody arpeggios. ‘Cadillac’ confirms its title with a Deep Southern twang, while ‘Der Photograph’ chirps like a computer, or perhaps snaps like a camera shutter. Alvear plays the pieces in such a way as to clearly distinguish between climbing like a vine (‘1 Fehler’) and like a staircase (‘Fahrplan’). The second disc, containing only three pieces but lasting almost as long as the first, shows how Frey’s music increased in openness and lightness over the years, before turning something of a corner, as heard in the recent title piece composed for Alvear. A feeling that keeps coming back to me as I listen is that this music isn’t ‘pared down’ or stripped back to the essentials, but rather constitutes the very most that Frey and Alvear were able to wrest from a given moment. Sometimes it isn’t enough, and sometimes it feels like an embarrassment of riches. Time and silence (tearing one from the other; one passing into the other; what is ever really one?) begin to merge. Jürg Frey Cristián Alvear Another Timbre

items._cn_summary: 这是一张由智利吉他演奏家克里斯蒂安·阿尔维阿录制、瑞士作曲家于尔格·弗雷创作的吉他独奏双碟专辑。第一碟收录1989年的《50 Sächelchen》（50件小物），由50首短曲组成，涵盖旋律性乐句、下行音型、长持续音及忧郁琶音等多种风格，甚至出现南方乡村式滑音与相机快门般的节奏片段。第二碟仅含三首作品，篇幅却与第一碟接近，展现了弗雷音乐在岁月中逐步走向更开阔与轻盈的演变轨迹，收尾是为阿尔维阿创作的首本曲同名作。整张专辑的演奏极为克制内敛，单音如石子落入沉默之池，回响消散后才迎来下一个声响。乐评指出，作品并非被'削减'至本质，而是演奏者与作曲家从当下瞬间所能攫取的最丰富内容，沉默与时间在音乐中不断交融。音乐中隐约可辨巴洛克与西班牙古典吉他的回声痕迹，但始终不固化为任何确定的旋律或抽象。

items.body: Honoring its title, Justyna Jablonska‘s Unforeseen never heads exactly where expected; in fact, it’s not even close. The cellist’s debut solo album drips with the confidence of exploration, incorporating multiple genres while acting as a metaphor for the immigrant experience. Jablonska connects the migration of birds with the migration of people and the migration of oft-improvised notes, focusing on the lives of Ukrainian, Polish and Roma Gypsy migrants. While this seems like a lot to tackle, the artist does so with aplomb. The album begins as one might expect a cellist’s album to begin, with sedate phrasing, multitracked lines and a regal tone. The title track demonstrates Jablonska’s depth of emotion while establishing the baseline from which it will soon wander. Were the record to have continued in this vein, it would have remained exemplary; yet the artist strives for something greater, just as those dreaming for a better life might pack their belongings, imitating the flocks passing overhead in the spring and fall. As “If You Can Hear This” launches with a spoken word sample and jungle rhythms, all bets are off. The artist will not be confined by expectation. Is it safe? Not at all, and therein lies the appeal. The bird, the immigrant, the artist may each be called upon to adapt to new surroundings. “9 Daughers” is the first of three vocal pieces, beginning in birdsong and proceeding to a rendition of a traditional Lithuanian folk song A linden tree has nine branches, each one corresponding to a daughter, who each in turn are married, leaving the mother to “sweep the ashes.” The tone is one of mingled celebration and sadness: the empty nest, the broken tree. Can even the birds sing the sorrow away? The next piece starts with the sound of traffic, implying movement; then peaceful kalimba, cello and electronics, each in turn moving the music further away from its origins. The skies open in “Wayward,” and Jablonska seems forlorn, until a series of upbeat melodies are translated to percussion and string. These are the unforeseen joys of leaving the place where one has begun; by the end, the skies have cleared. But not all changes are easy; “Fabryka” introduces a brief note of dissonance, setting the listener up for Monika Niemczynowicz’s return on “The Pact,” an extremely dark cautionary tale from Roztocze, Poland. The presence of such songs underlines the connection between land, culture and memory ~ tales passed down generation to generation, even when the family has migrated to a new home. One hungers for the live show, incorporating film and copious amounts of spoken word, hinted at in the final minute of “Procession.” The album’s greatest surprise arrives toward the end with “Shchedryk (feat. Sofiia Fylypiv).” Most listeners will recognize “Carol of the Bells” in an instant, and many will recall its Ukrainian origins, but few will remember that the song predates Christianity and is about a swallow wishing a family “prosperity, good fortune and a fruitful year.” Jablonska reinstates the original title and meaning, reclaiming it from distortion. This too is a metaphor for the immigrant experience: the temptation to integrate to the extent that one’s history is sublimated. Jablonska, who lives in Glasgow, closes with her own take on “The Skye Boat Song,” which was itself adapted from a Gaelic tune. By the end, one is wondering about the the tug between one’s national origin and country of residence, and the very definition of home. (Richard Allen)

items._cn_summary: 大提琴家贾布洛夫斯卡首张个人专辑以迁徙为核心隐喻，将鸟类迁徙、移民经历与即兴音符的流动并置，关注乌克兰、波兰及罗姆吉普赛移民议题。作品从沉稳的大提琴织体出发，标题曲展现深厚情感基调，随后大胆引入碎拍节奏与口语采样，彻底打破传统大提琴专辑的预期框架。专辑收录三首人声作品，其中立陶宛民歌以鸟类鸣唱引出母亲目送九女出嫁的悲喜交织叙事；旅人形象贯穿全篇，拇指琴、电子音效与弦乐层层叠加，将音乐推离原点。波兰方言民俗故事与乌克兰传统颂歌的加入，使唱片承载土地、文化与记忆的代际传递，作为跨界融合的当代古典实验作品展现出难能可贵的艺术胆识与文化深度。

items.body: Simon Heath closes the release notes with “May you rest in peace.” There’s nothing to add to that. The Yasu Ether Project is an overall haunting and pleasant experience, a final document of an artist who understood that darkness and stillness aren’t opposites of beauty but conditions under which a particular kind of beauty becomes possible. César Alexandre knew that instinctively, and this album proves it one last time. A quiet closing chapter The Yasu Ether Project by Mount Shrine   Cryo Chamber has held the bar for exploratory dark ambient music with a cinematic edge since Simon Heath (the artist behind Atrium Carceri) founded the label with a collaborative focus that has become its defining characteristic. The catalog spans deep space drone, horror-influenced soundscapes, Lovecraftian collaborative projects, and the kind of patient, immersive dark ambient that rewards extended, solitary listening. Among its most beloved artists was Mount Shrine—the project of César Alexandre, a Brazilian producer from Rio de Janeiro who grew up absorbing Brian Eno, Burial, Aphex Twin, and Akira Yamaoka‘s score for Silent Hill 2 before finding his own voice in lo-fi field recordings, vinyl crackle, tape hiss, and long meditative drone structures. He debuted on Cryo Chamber with Winter Restlessness in 2018, followed by Ghosts on Broken Pavements in 2019. He also worked under Mount Hibiki and released vaporwave under the name Lindsheaven Virtual Plaza, an early and influential figure in that scene. César Alexandre passed away on April 15, 2021, from COVID-19. He was one of the first artists whose work made people fall in love with ambient music, and the void he left has been felt consistently in the years since. Cryo Chamber has honored his memory carefully—releasing All Roads Lead Home in 2022 and The Mount Hibiki Tapes in 2024, and The Yasu Ether Project arrives now as the final piece of audio he ever sent to Simon Heath. A version had previously appeared on his own Bandcamp before the page closed. Now preserved and released once more, it stands as a quiet closing chapter. There is a somber feeling that comes with reading about this release before you press play, and that feeling doesn’t leave once you do. Listening to this is the last remnant of his feelings and emotions, the final transmission from an artist whose music offered rest, solitude, and quiet escape to everyone who found it. Just like most Cryo Chamber releases you can expect a very dark and soft ride through the entirety of the album, but there is something that peaks through all the darkness, a simple peace that is haunting. You don’t know what it is that’s calming about it. Maybe it’s the field recordings of birds and daytime, the remembrance of what it feels like when you’ve just woken from a bad storm. Unsettling and peaceful at the same time. That’s how it feels listening to this. Unsettling and peaceful at the same time :: “Gaseous Peak” and “Polysunset” are the standouts on this release. The entirety of the album is wrapped in vinyl hiss, that persistent crackle that was always central to Mount Shrine‘s identity, the sound of something being played back from a medium that’s been worn down by time. It gives the record a physical texture, a sense that these recordings exist in a material world even as the music itself drifts away from one. The closing track is something different. The synths here aren’t just simple pads and atmospheric textures like the rest of the album. Little vocal touches, small nothings, barely registered, appear as the pads build. A small key arp plays in and out, and the visual being created in your head as you listen is genuinely peaceful in a way that feels earned after everything that preceded it. The contradiction at the heart of this closing track is what makes it so affecting, the familiar Mount Shrine darkness is still present, but something lighter has been let in, a crack of warmth that sits differently knowing what this release represents. Simon Heath closes the release notes with “May you rest in peace.” There’s nothing to add to that. The Yasu Ether Project is an overall haunting and pleasant experience, a final document of an artist who understood that darkness and stillness aren’t opposites of beauty but conditions under which a particular kind of beauty becomes possible. César Alexandre knew that instinctively, and this album proves it one last time. The Yasu Ether Project is available on Cryo Chamber. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是巴西制作人César Alexandre（Mount Shrine）于2021年因COVID-19去世后遗留下来的最后一批音频作品，由Cryo Chamber厂牌发行。作为一张遗作专辑，它延续了Mount Shrine标志性的创作路径：低保真田野录音、黑胶底噪、磁带嘶声与长时冥想型无人机结构交织在一起。整张专辑保持Cryo Chamber一贯的暗黑柔软质地，但贯穿始终的是一种难以名状的宁静感——鸟鸣与白昼环境音若隐若现，仿佛暴风过后的短暂平静。评论者指出作品同时具备不安与平和的双重特质，这种矛盾的张力正是其最动人的地方。乐评同时梳理了César Alexandre从Brian Eno、Burial、Silent Hill 2配乐中汲取养分、最终在lo-fi田野录音与冥想无人机领域形成个人语汇的艺术轨迹，也提及他作为早期vaporwave场景代表人物的多面身份。专辑既是个人艺术生涯的终章，也是对一位在暗氛围音乐领域留下深刻印记的创作者的纪念。

items.body: Six tracks, no wasted motion. ARKADA005 doesn’t revive electro; it plugs it back in, turns the voltage up, and lets the machine speak for itself. Drawing on the foundational grammar of electro Marking a welcome return to the furor of contemporary electronic music, London’s Arkada resurfaces with ARKADA005, a six-track workout from Brussels’ Arsonist Recorder and Sigma. This is electro with the futurist chrome stripped back enough to expose the working parts: rolling bass, snapping breaks, brutal low-end pressure and melodies that still know how to carry a tune. The record feels contemporary without straining to prove it, drawing on the foundational grammar of electro while treating that grammar as ​something alive, flexible and available for further damage. Arsonist Recorder takes the first three cuts straight to the machine soul. The rhythms are tight but never sterile, with heavyweight bass movement and synth lines that bring a real sense of propulsion. There is funk here, but it is not nostalgia-funk. It is the physical intelligence of the form: music built to make the body respond while the circuitry does something stranger underneath. Sigma answers with three tracks that feel like an autopsy performed at club volume. The components are stripped down, isolated and rebuilt into lean, muscular constructions where breaks, bass and synthetic detail lock together with increasingly brutal efficiency. What makes the record work is the tension between its opposing instincts—sweet melody and hard mechanics, precision and abrasion, body-popping unity and 4am chicanery. Six tracks, no wasted motion. ARKADA005 doesn’t revive electro; it plugs it back in, turns the voltage up, and lets the machine speak for itself. Arkada #005 is available on Arkada. items._cn_summary: 这张六曲split EP由布鲁塞尔两位电子音乐人Arsonist Recorder与Sigma分别贡献三首作品，延续electro这一电子舞曲传统的根基语法，但以更具当代感和机械感的方式重新处理。Arsonist Recorder的前三首强调紧密节奏与重型低音推进，合成器线条带有真正的推力感，funk元素并非怀旧模仿而是形式本身的物理智能。Sigma的后三首将声音组件拆解、隔离并重组为精瘦有力的结构，断片与低音的咬合愈发凶猛高效。整张专辑的张力来自甜美的旋律与硬质机械感、精度与摩擦、身体律动与凌晨四点的暗流之间的对峙。不试图复活electro，而是将其重新通电、调高电压，让机器自己发声。

items.body: Durable Oxide announces itself with DOX-001—the debut release from a new Portland, Oregon-based label intent on delivering decisive electronic atmospheres. It’s a strong opening statement for a label to make, and Radio Free Money earns it. Textured electronic music with an edge of menace Radio Free Money by Latest Fad   Durable Oxide announces itself with DOX-001—the debut release from a new Portland, Oregon-based label intent on delivering decisive electronic atmospheres. It’s a strong opening statement for a label to make, and Radio Free Money earns it. For a first release, the RIYL speaks volumes: Demdike Stare, Stars of the Lid, The Heartwood Institute, Castles In Space. That’s a specific compass pointing toward slow-burn, cinematic, deeply textured electronic music with an edge of menace, and Latest Fad delivers exactly that. Latest Fad is a duo—Paul Uusitalo and Dan Wilk, members based in Portland, OR and Seattle, WA, who have been collaborating on professional video software together for decades before turning their full attention to music in earnest in 2019. Their previous two albums came out on their own imprint Fading Systems. Radio Free Money is the​ir third full-length and their first on an outside label, employing banks of antiquated synthesizers, modern workstations, analog effects devices, and stringed instruments woven into an electroacoustic pastiche of submerged melodies, hidden rhythms, drops that never arrive, and hopeful/mournful atmospherics. The description “both claustrophobic and infinitely expansive” is apt—this is music that feels like it’s pressing in and opening outward at the same time. Simple ambience, but it works :: At first, Latest Fad is genuinely mysterious—you don’t know what to expect when you press play. This leans toward the ambient experimental side of things but has melodic aspects woven through. “Business Hugs II” arrives as the second track and introduces a static stutter effect that’s immediately intriguing, it opens a conversation the rest of the album keeps having with itself. This plays more as a collective than a conventional album, tracks functioning as interconnected environments rather than separate songs. “Overgrowth Mindset” is one of the most melodic pieces on the release—keys, off-rhythmic tones, and a bassline that brings some light into what is otherwise a consistently dark listening experience. Simple ambience, but it works as contrast against the heavier material surrounding it. “Aberrant Tool & Die” is another interesting piece—its only rhythm is a stable boom with a building single-note cymbal hit, that stale one-note repetition becoming hypnotic as other sounds and effects surface in the background before the track ends in a very dark place. Restraint is the operative word here. The track knows what not to do, and that’s half the work. “Live Laugh Loop” is the favorite of the release—a sad, dark melody with a flanged note sweeping in that makes the intro deliberately hard to parse. The distortion on the pads creates a density that almost obscures the other elements underneath, but those elements are there and they emerge gradually. Nothing here follows a conventional melodic pattern. The only thing obeying musical note rules is the distorted pads themselves—everything surrounding it is off-tone, and that off-tone quality is exactly what gives the track its dark, closing character. As a final statement it lands well. For a label’s debut release, Durable Oxide has set a clear and credible tone. Labels like Castles In Space and The Heartwood Institute built their identities one carefully chosen release at a time, letting the catalog define the aesthetic rather than announcing it upfront. DOX-001 suggests Durable Oxide understands that logic. Radio Free Money is a strong opening argument for what the label intends to be. Radio Free Money is available on Durable Oxide. items.body: The German duo Arnte and Schmoun—formerly active together as Nordschlacht and Ugh, but having operated as Pyrroline for years—are releasing their fifth album, “Ambiguity”. The work appears inspired by the world we live in and, above all, by the impact of various events on the human psyche. Musically, this translates into 12 tracks that immediately reveal the signature Pyrroline sound. The group remains closely linked to the musical legacy of early Skinny Puppy. Hovering somewhere between sophisticated EBM and atmospheric Dark-Electro, this new opus once again succeeds in captivating the listener. A dark, frenzied atmosphere is established, underpinned by complex percussion. At times, the mood is somewhat tormented, yet that is precisely the strength of certain tracks. The polished production features a wealth of sounds and subtle effects, layered with ghostly vocals. Here and there, female vocals appear, adding a touch of cold sensuality. One of the tracks also features a collaboration with TC75. “Ambiguity” may not be the band’s strongest album—their previous release, “Struggling”, was a masterpiece, after all—but it remains a powerful record from a group that, in my opinion, continues to be somewhat underrated. (Rating:8). Listen to “Eventually”: https://electroaggressionrecords.bandcamp.com/track/eventually

items.body: On Sundays, we like to take the opportunity to share something aside from an album review, like interviews we've conducted or videos that we have found and enjoyed, and sometimes, something entirely different, like liner notes. The following notes, written by Paul Acquaro, accompany the adventurous duo release Treasures Within by Harri Sjöström and Guilherme Rodrigues. This album is the second document of the duo following The Treasures Are . The Treasures Within is comprised of three encounters in the studio and live starting in 2019 at Munich's Artoxin Gallery followed by the Berlin locations Toolbox Gallery in 2021 and Berlin Room in 2022. By Paul Acquaro What makes musical chemistry? What is it that make some combinations simply work? While there are many examples like Paul and John, Bennink and Brotzmann, and Parker and Drake to draw on, it also seems that saxophonist Harri Sjöström and cellist Guilherme Rodrigues have some insights into this phenomenon as well. Here, it begins with creaky bow strokes on the cello to which squeaky tones from a soprano saxophone are carefully inserted. It lasts only a minute before a reset, the next track and a new route chosen, but in those previous few seconds one could hear a lot about a musical relationship. There is no hesitancy, no time needed to discuss and calibrate, it is a meeting of mutually sympathetic musical minds. Rodrigues explains, "for me the way Harri approaches the saxophone gets pretty close, imagination wise, to my imaginarium. And because of that, we play well together intuitively." The next track begins with a rather classical sounding approach and then quickly becomes an intertwining of melodic strands that are in some ways hard to differentiate, but thrive on an inherent contrast. Rodrigues continues, "both instruments have colors that naturally match and therefore, taken together, the result of our music becomes treasured!" Indeed, by the time we are at track 3, which happens quickly with these miniatures, the melodic ideas have taken a different turn. Sjöström is bouncing around a delicate melodic idea while Rodrigues provides textural accents. Suddenly, we are at track 4 and now the cello is responsible for the melodic twists while the saxophone finds the perfect points to interject. Sjöström also gives some hints as to why this pairing works so well, "I think we both share a strong melodic instinct, even within freely improvised music. There is a constant dialogue between us, and I always feel Guilherme is incredibly alert to every subtle change in the music." So, what is it about these subtle changes that are so powerful? Well, for one, the conversation is always diverting course. Like on track 5, which suddenly turns inwards, darker hues and longer tones fill the space. Sjöström simply says, "we also enjoy strong contrasts and often abrupt changes and aren't afraid to move between intimacy and intensity." < Please go to Bandcamp to read the rest of the notes and listen to the music > Email This BlogThis! items._cn_summary: 《Treasures Within》是Harri Sjöström（高音萨克斯）与Guilherme Rodrigues（大提琴）合作的第二张作品，录音跨越2019至2022年三个场地：慕尼黑Artoxin Gallery、柏林Toolbox Gallery及柏林Room。专辑由三段录音中提炼出的短小片段组成，每段约一分钟左右即转入下一轨。两位乐手以自由即兴为核心，萨克斯的尖锐高音与大提琴的弓弦摩擦声形成微妙对话，展现出极强的直觉默契。大提琴常负责旋律线条的走向，萨克斯则在恰当的间隙插入音色与质感；乐句之间频繁出现强烈的明暗对比与突变，从亲密的低语骤然转入暗沉的绵长音调。音乐家本人强调双方共享强烈的旋律本能，即使在完全自由的框架中也能保持对话的连贯性，乐器音色天然互补。这张专辑呈现的是欧洲地下即兴场景中两位乐手之间高度敏锐的互动关系。

items.body: Leo‘s latest six-track EP, Cicada Burnt, is a stunningly crafted collection of teknoid soundscapes where cutting-edge pulses scatter love bullets of intent with serious depth, weight and imagination. A cinematic ascent that feels simultaneously weightless Cicada Burnt by leo   Leo‘s latest six-track EP, Cicada Burnt, is a stunningly crafted collection of teknoid soundscapes where cutting-edge pulses scatter love bullets of intent with serious depth, weight and imagination. If electronic music came as cakes, this would be a deeply delicious one: richly layered, beautifully balanced and full of rewarding detail with every return. Expansive atmospheres form the broad canvas upon which pole and wood basslines stutter in and out of half-time, dub-inflected drops, while slack hi-hats and clipped synth motifs generate an insistent sixteenth-note tension that constantly nudges the music forwards without ever overcrowding it. Opener “Qwershapes” immediately establishes the EP’s language, balancing precision with abandon in a thrilling display of rhythmic confidence and sonic restraint. “Jetti” follows by treating emptiness, timing and negative space as instruments in themselves, exemplifying the post-genre spirit increasingly defining contemporary elec​tronics. Rather than merely hopping between stylistic traditions from one track to the next, Leo folds those traditions into individual compositions, dissolving tribal boundaries with the confidence of an artist more interested in expression than categorization. The title track is a genuine low-end masterwork. Wah-soaked synths, sculpted percussion, clipped rhythmic fragments and heavyweight bass converge into something simultaneously playful and profound, expressing the paradox that the deepest seriousness often reveals itself through the joy of creative play. It is music that feels instinctive rather than calculated, communicating an artistic presence that cannot simply be learned. “Descant” reinforces that philosophy through muscular bass pressure and hypnotic propulsion before the closing two-part “Spirit Level” reaches the record’s emotional summit. “Prescript” inhabits an elusive territory between ambience, dub, found sound and bass music without settling into any recognizable form, its immense scale matched by genuine warmth. The concluding piece channels skyscraper tension, unstable bass movements, dub-wise pyrotechnics and voice-like pads into a cinematic ascent that feels simultaneously weightless and earthbound. Superb work, and comfortably one of the finest releases in Leo‘s growing catalog. Cicada Burnt is available on Peak Oil. items.body: Across eight tracks, Germano channels a stunning miasma of electronic and acoustic instrumentation, art-house aesthetics, and installation-worthy musical spaces. Balancing precision with emotional ambiguity opera23 is Vincenzo Germano who, after an apparent three-year hiatus, returns to Wic Recordings with Teatro Armónico—a valiant, mature statement of adult aural dynamics. Across eight tracks, Germano channels a stunning miasma of electronic and acoustic instrumentation, art-house aesthetics, and installation-worthy musical spaces. Grand piano discordance sits alongside elevated musicianship, while glitch techniques fracture and elevate the compositions rather than simply decorate them. Every movement feels carefully considered, balancing precision with emotional ambiguity. Rather than chasing convention, Teatro Armónico unfolds as a sequence of immersive environments where composition, texture, and silence carry equal weight. Organic performances dissolve into digital erosion before reforming in unexpected ways, creating a dialogue between the human hand and machine inter​vention. The result is music that rewards patient listening, revealing new details with every return. This is neither academic abstraction nor easy ambience. Germano occupies the fertile ground between contemporary classical composition, electroacoustic experimentation, and sound art, producing an album that is intellectually engaging without sacrificing feeling. Teatro Armónico is a quietly commanding return—one that confirms opera23 as an artist more interested in lasting resonance than fleeting impact. TEATRO ARMÓNICO is available on Wic. items.body: It took no less than nine years for the new opus from Swiss band Sleepwalk to arrive. Founder Bruno Rush, assisted by Andreas Lehmann, has prepared 15 new tracks for “Dystopia”. An additional disc featuring no fewer than 17 is also available. To say the wait was long is an understatement, but it was certainly worth it. The result, “Dystopia”, is truly impressive. Sleepwalk’s compositions straddle the line between EBM and Dark-Electro. The songwriting is highly sophisticated, backed by an impressive sonic arsenal. The atmosphere is dark and the rhythms are danceable, while the tracks manage to be complex yet accessible. On the standout tracks—and there are quite a few—you can hear influences from the early Canadian EBM school; I am thinking specifically of the genius of Skinny Puppy. The opening tracks, in particular, absolutely blew me away and, in my opinion, rank among the best material Sleepwalk has ever produced. Given that the band has been active since 1992 and has a substantial back catalogue, the long wait has truly paid off. Sleepwalk hasn’t reinvented itself; rather, they seem to have taken a step back to reflect on their future direction. Lehmann’s haunting vocals fit the album’s atmosphere and genre perfectly. Towards the end, a few more magnificent tracks emerge, evoking the sound of Front Line Assembly. And then, of course, there’s the bonus disc, featuring 14 bands, each contributing a cover of a Sleepwalk song, plus three remixes by three different bands. It’s quite unusual to see so many bands featured with covers rather than remixes, and the least I can say is that it’s a very original idea—and it works. There’s also a fine lineup of artists assembled here, including labelmates such as Pyroline, Trilogy, T.A.N.K., Serpents, and Synaptic Defect, as well as EBM scene veterans such as Plastic Noise Experience, Brain Leisure, Individual Totem, R010R, Pantser Fabriek, To Avoid, and others. I have to say, there are some brilliant songs to be heard. Plastic Noise Experience does a fantastic job on “Afterlife,” and I should also mention Individual Totem, Synaptic Defect, and Nine Seconds. “Dystopia” is an album with a strong nostalgic streak, yet one that has been successfully translated into a powerful, contemporary sound: tormented EBM featuring some highly danceable tracks. Sleepwalk is back, and the world is going to know it. Side-Line announced the release in April 2026 in Sleepwalk return with ‘Dystopia’ 2CD on Electro Aggression Records, which listed the 2CD and digital editions and the full remix roster of the bonus disc “Interpretations”. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Devil In Disguise”: Devil in Disguise by Sleepwalk About Sleepwalk Sleepwalk are a dark electro and EBM act from Bern, Switzerland. The project was founded in 1992 by Oliver Spring and Bruno Ruch, Andreas Lehmann, and Charly of tEaR!doWn. The group started releasing material in the early 1990s, including “Immortal Disease” from 1994, the first album “Door To Insomnia…” in 1995 on Khazad-Dûm, “Black Diagnose” in 1999, “Torture Chamber” in 2002, “Retrospect 94-96 (The Early Years)” in 2003, and “Rapid Eye Movement” on Scanner in March 2004. By the mid-2000s the lineup had shifted. Oliver Spring left the band in 2005. The band later released the EP “Revenge Of The Lost” in 2011 and the concept album “Nibiru” in 2012, both on Scanner. Sleepwalk joined Electro Aggression Records to release “Tempus Vincit Omnia” on January 3, 2018. The band said they wanted to move back toward more classic dark electro with EBM influence after “Nibiru”. The Bandcamp-only digital set “Remakes”, issued on April 11, 2026, revisited older Sleepwalk tracks ahead of “Dystopia”, the 2CD set reviewed here.

items.body: The “distractions” of Greg Kelley’s trumpet and Yoona Kim’s ajaeng on this new album for Relative Pitch are hardly simple diversions for the listener, as one often thinks about the term. Actually, I find the music on this lovely duet recording to be at various times quieting, disruptive, disturbing, and even a challenge. Listeners familiar with Greg Kelley’s recorded output will not be shocked by what they hear, and at times this album reminds me a great deal of the trumpet player’s provocative, whisper-improvising duo Nmperign. Actually, the other half of that duo, Bhob Rainey, mixed and mastered Distractions . Kelley performs wonderfully and utilizes a reticence that nearly always prevents him from easily erupting into high energy bursts. His patience and discipline are admirable. The unexplored story here, however, is ajaeng player Yoona Kim. I was not familiar with Kim’s instrument of choice, and this reality is part of what first drew me to this recording. An ajaeng is a Korean zither-like instrument–think a bendier, more temperamental cello laid on its back. It can be plucked, but is often bowed with a stick or a more standard Western bow of horsehair. Kim is a polymath of musical styles and performs at least seven distinct genres, according to her website. Free improvisation and jazz are two of these, as are contemporary and traditional Korean music. The others are more surprising: Delta Blues, Klezmer, and Appalachian Old-Time Music. Despite an extensive set of online live performances, Kim is still relatively young and has only three recordings as a leader to her name. Distractions is one of these, and the other two, Deltat Dokkaebi and Modern Gagok, are all but impossible to find. A strong outing with pianist Anthony Coleman can be viewed here . This dazzling performance has a mere 25 views and 2 likes as of this writing. Free Jazz Blog readers, you know what to do. With all this being said, Yoona Kim is particularly challenging to define, though she has performed in some of the revered free jazz spaces (The Stone, for a week-long residence in July of 2026) and studied or played with many names readers of the FJC are quite familiar with: Tom Rainey, Chris Corsano, Joe Morris, and Linda May Han Oh. And of course, Greg Kelley. Distractions for Trumpet and Ajaeng is a wonderful album, full of quiet restraint and unsettling surprises. While the opening track, “Display,” starts with insistent blowing and bending, the first minute and a half is about as busy as the album gets. Kim bows and pulls the strings of her ajaeng while Greg Kelley flutters a raspy, metallic horn down into registers so low and frequencies so wobbly I had to stop the music to see if something was wrong with my speakers. The aesthetic largely, however, is quiet. To be more precise, silence that alternates with tiny eruptions of activity. Listen to the second track, the lovely “Dispute,” for this as Yoona Kim rips and bows urgently just before the one minute mark, at which point the recording falls into total silence. When the musicians return, Greg Kelley is more active and works his way into an exploration of one wavering note. This interplay builds as the two play an eerie high-harmony fit for hungry ghosts that largely bends and vibrates as it squeals and scrapes. While the dynamics never really reach the loudest of volumes, all of this silence makes certain mid-level insertions of noise jarring. For example, on my favorite piece on the album, the closer “Disappear,” Kelley forces air through his horn with such subtle power, and balances a series of soft notes so sinister, that my dog ran out of the room when I first played it. This, of course, is the power of understatement, and the album as a whole serves as a wonderful reminder that so often in music, as in our day-to-day laboring, what produces joy or excitement, as well as heaviness, sorrow, or surprise is how the moments fall together. Distractions is a delight of quiet echoes and disquieting interruptions that is well worth the listen. Distractions for Trumpet & Ajaeng by Greg Kelley and Yoona Kim Email This BlogThis! items.body:
“The thing about playing the tuba in an orchestra is that you don’t have to play that much,” admitted composer Matthew Wright, who grew up playing the tuba in orchestras and funk bands, “but it’s the best seat in the house. You hear music back to front. The percussion and the brass are loud, so you hear all their detail, and the strings are this kind of ethereal thing that’s off in the distance.”

For the Kent-based Wright, who also improvises using turntables, samplers, and processers – most impactfully with Trance Map, his partnership with Evan Parker – this early realization nurtured a sensibility leading to the creation of immersive works that mix composition, improvisation, and technology. Cracked Glaze (False Walls) is a case in point, as it utilizes notated material – “dot music” is his good-humored term – improvisation, and Wright’s real-time sampling and processing immediately fed into surround sound, all of which he remixed for the CD.

Wright’s collaborators on Cracked Glaze represent various facets of his work. Ensemble Klang, an ensemble of mostly Dutch new music virtuosi, was an early champion of Wright’s compositions. Spheric Totemic is a Wright-instigated, flexibly configured improvising group with, on this occasion, Mandhira de Saram, Alexander Hawkins, Neil Charles and Stephen Davis. Sofia Jernberg, whose Musho with Hawkins was one of the brighter lights of 2024, is new to Wright’s constellation.

Historically, the conventional wisdom among exponents of freely improvised music is that the larger the group, the more apt the music will be muddied. It is a yardstick that is also prevalent among practitioners of contemporary composition. Individuality – of the improviser, of the composer – is more difficult to assert in or through a crowd. Although there are more than a dozen musicians heard on Cracked Glaze, there is no nebulous sprawl or complexity for complexity’s sake. Abstraction is tethered to figuration, the spine of the piece being a descending line that repeatedly submerges and reemerges, giving the interactions of voices clear relationships.

“In a lot of my written work for ensembles there is a central concern that tends to last a long period of time, an idea that will give the piece structure. I’m really interested in music being a kind of terrain that you can hear through and around, so that when you are listening, you are experiencing a kind of ‘visual’ situation. I guess this goes back to my work with vinyl records, because records make music a physical surface, where you can place the needle anywhere in the terrain of the music.

“In the improvised work, I don’t want to be the guy that says to improvisers, ‘this is how it goes.’ Improvisation, in a free context, is about distributed leadership. It’s about this beautiful situation of people saying, ‘the music could go here’ or ‘I hear the future of this music in what you’re playing,’ and the kind of listening that leads to those sorts of situations.

“Having the opportunity to work with a group that is mainly readers – Ensemble Klang – and a group that is mainly improvisers – Spheric Totemic – and Sofia Jernberg, gave me the opportunity to do something I haven’t done much of in my music, to have a spine that is unfurling but is always there. It doesn’t necessarily always have to be the main focus of the piece, but it will always be there. It will structure time in a certain way; improvisers can do whatever they want to do, and the music will be as much about them as it is the spine. I was really interested in having a sort of ‘object’ in the space of the improvisation. It’s almost like in the visual art world, where you have people moving around in a gallery but there’s a sculpture there. It’s in the room with you.”

Another virtue of Cracked Glaze is that it is the type of work that initially seems to come out of nowhere. It smacks of singularity. However, Wright’s backstory reveals that he did not come out of nowhere, as he has a pedigree linking him to England’s most consequential institutional incubator of experimental music, as well as its most venerable, living exponent of improvised music. Both associations largely account for how Wright’s disparate interests – several of which were common among Gen Xers in their formative years but were delayed in being assimilated into experimental music – were shaped into a mature aesthetic, and yielded in Cracked Glaze an arguably definitive statement.

“My experience, first of all, was writing music and playing in brass bands and funk bands and small improvising groups with friends,” Wright recently explained. “But I also liked writing chamber music for people who would take it away and play it somewhere else. I might not even be there for the performance. This background took me to study at the University of Huddersfield with the Professor who set up the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival, Richard Steinitz. I was very lucky. It was kind of random. He was my composition teacher. So, I was very lucky to have experiences like knocking on the door for a composition lesson and Richard Steinitz saying, ‘Ah, Matt, I can’t possibly teach you right now, but meet Karlheinz,’ and the door opens and there’s this world-famous composer from another generation that I had read about, but never dreamed I would meet.

“Contemporary classical music was a big part of my education, but I DJed as a kid. I was really interested at that point in the ‘80s and ‘90s when software, sampling, and DJ technology, was becoming affordable. It started showing up in people’s homes. Contemporary classical music and DJ culture were colliding in my mind when I was a kid. The only kind of formal education I could get was a classical education, along with some jazz theory, but it was largely based on dot music, written music. Then there was this other (non-written) side, like DJ culture and all of the great heritage of Black music that DJ culture is part of, and that was a kind of informal education I studied for myself.

“When I was a real little kid – like 12 or 13 – I made a lot of bedroom productions with a basic computer and turntable setup, really focused on instrumental hip-hop. I started to scratch around then, just watching how it was done on TV. My main inspirations were DJ Premier of Gangstarr, Terminator X of Public Enemy, and Maseo of De La Soul. When I was around 18 or 19, as a student, I DJed for a few parties, playing mainly funk, hip hop, and drum ‘n' bass. Around the same time – 1996-98 – I was in a few pop/funk bands that needed a DJ, so I did a few things with beat juggling and matching the pitch of the horns with turntable scratches, etc.

“In 1999 I DJed for a social event at the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival and I decided to just play fragments of music that I loved at the time: The Jazz Warriors, Louis Andriessen, Loose Tubes, Squarepusher, Björk. On the basis of that weird mix, I got the call to DJ at Abbey Road for the launch of a music charity, the PRS Foundation, in 2000. That was both a social event and included some (not entirely successful!) experimental scratching. When I moved to Holland to study with composer Louis Andriessen in 2002, I joined a trio with laptop artist Tom Tlalim and saxophonist Keir Neuringer – now of Irreversible Entanglements – and we played a few house parties and small gigs with our own mix of free improv and beat-based electronica. That same year the Huddersfield Festival commissioned ‘Presents from an Edited Then’ which was a 70-minute piece for The Apollo Saxophone Quartet and me DJing, designed for a club venue, again a mix of ‘social’ and ‘experimental’. That’s when I got interested in the worlds of contemporary classical music and DJ culture colliding.”

One of the first projects Wright embarked on was to compose for turntables and to teach classically-trained percussionists how to use them, integrating John Cage’s early work for percussion with the innovations of Christian Marclay and Otomo Yoshihide. “In a piece called Contact Theatre I had literally written out all of the material for notation-reading percussionists”, Wright said of the work. “If you look at a musical stave with the four spaces between the lines, I used those spaces to represent the four spaces on a vinyl record. The space that would be a F in the treble stave, that’s the space on the outer edge of the record, before any musical material appears on the vinyl record. All of the musical material on the record is included in the second space, and then the space at the center of the record was the third space, and then the label itself in the fourth space. You can prepare those spaces, put stickers on them. I would literally write percussion rhythms and they could produce those rhythms by dropping the needle on the record and get a ricochet effect or specify a section of the record I want to be played, say a saxophone solo three minutes into the record. I developed these ‘half-contact’ techniques where the needle sticks like a locked groove, and I taught the basics of hip hop scratching to percussionists, even though the music didn’t sound anything like hip hop.”

Wright then began to assess the proportions of and the relationships between the elements of his aesthetic and how to integrate them in his work. “Cracked Glaze is a collision of all of the above. I have been doing ensemble work and turntable work and installation work, but a lot of my focus is on the work with Evan in mixing and even post-production of the Trance Map material. Post-production is really part of the process, and Evan is very interested in exploring all that. Although Cracked Glaze doesn’t involve Evan, it brings to equal terms all of the sources I work with. There’s some notation written for Ensemble Klang with holes in that notation, space for the improvisation group of Spheric Totemic and Sofia Jernberg. They have start and stop times for the improvising, and they also sometimes have cues for some notation. I’m also mixing them live on stage, taking samples and remixing them and using the turntable as well. Then I take all that material and work on it a little in the studio, not to radically change the piece but to bring out some of the elements that you would hear live but not in a stereo recording. The piece brings together notation, improvisation, and technology, but not as separate forms. They all intersect. That’s where they all join on the map.”

In a roundabout way, the title of the piece speaks to the processes of its creation. It refers to the glazes used in high-fire ceramics that are formulated to crack on temperature; even though they are applied in an even manner, the cracking results in a surface that can be likened to a mosaic assembled with random tiles, with dark, hair-thin spaces between them. Though the results are subject to a unique firing, the experienced artist knows how to promote cracking that is pleasing and avoid cracking that ruins the piece.

“It may be interesting to talk about how jazz standards have worked in the past,” Wright responded to the idea of controlled cracking, and chuckling at the notion that he controlled the gas valve. “An excellent standard is one that can be played in its entirety and feel integrated and beautiful, but it is also a catalyst. It offers itself up to be cracked, to be turned into something new. In some ways, the use of notation to suggest a response is fascinating to me. On a technical level, there are definitely moments where I say to the improvisers, ‘at a certain point you will hear a line and at that point, that pitch, that’s your moment; if you’re improvising, the natural ebb and flow of the group will go to you’. But I don’t say ‘you should crack it’ to them; I say ‘it’s yours’.

“And there’s a third element there, the equivalent of the heat – the processing and the spatialization. I’m taking the feed of everybody, the notated music and the improvised music is coming to my setup, and I’m able to remix it and sample it. I’m an agent in the cracking, too. Whether it is notated or not is not the point, because it’s all going through the same system and being splintered into surround sound. That’s the third element, the sound design is a catalytic element.”

Wright pointed to a poster in his studio of a still influential Japanese textile exhibition he attended in his early 20s. “What I loved about that,” he said, “was that the dynamic shapes of these textiles are very rigid, spatially, but the textiles themselves have all sorts of holes in them. They are almost like fishing nets. I tried to create something similar by creating a structure that’s flexible but has holes in it. If we play this piece again, the melody line and the structure is going to be exactly the same every time and the improvising and the specialization will be different every time. That’s a long-winded way of saying I tried not to over notate.”

Wright acknowledged that post-production, particularly when the work was created in a surround sound environment and is remixed for stereo, creates a distinct experience of the work, and perhaps represents a new iteration of the pursuit of perfection in the studio, exemplified by Glenn Gould. “My pieces are concepts that have a sort of quantum existence,” Wright maintained. “What I mean is that if we are going to present the piece live, then there are circumstances that will be dynamic for the audience in the live space that may not be so dynamic when hearing it at home. In the live space, I’m dealing with surround sound. There are a whole lot of options to try to present that sort of experience in the stereo format. When it comes to making a CD or something online that people will listen to, I consider the domestic setting. I also consider that many people listen to music on the go, with headphones or their phone. You may be walking down the Avenue of the Americas and everything around you is changing, but there’s one consistent thread in the music.

“You have to consider the multiple ways that people listen now. I do hope that people will sit at home to listen to it. In that situation, it’s much closer to reading a book because it’s a solitary experience. You’re sitting with it for 40 or 50 minutes. Wearing headphones creates an interior experience. I really treasure those kinds of listeners and it’s a real privilege when someone spends that time with something that I’ve made with my musical friends.

“In the history of improvised music there have been many vehement statements about the relationship between free improvised music and recording. I totally get that, but I suppose that the question we now have to consider is what happens when you improvise with a recording. We don’t want the karaoke thing! How does the recording come back into the improvised music experience in as fluid a way you would have with another musician with an instrument? An instrument is obviously a technology of its own and the recording is the result of the technology. We need to make sure the technology is as flexible as any other instrument. The other thing I’m really fascinated by in the history of free creative music is the evolution of incorporating electronics. It’s really interesting for me when an electro-acoustic improvised situation might suggest that the music is not happening in the present tense, but in the past or the future.

“The thing I’m really interested in is those previously separated camps of notation, improvisation, and technology becoming one and the same, where there is an equaling out of the three. You’re not relying on one form of expression. And this seems to be causing a real revitalization of the scene, where people are mastering their separate disciplines and are also negotiating with each other. I think there’s more opportunity for creative music because of the dialogue between notation, improvisation, and technology. Looking for the connections between them is the main creative impetus. It’s not paper; it’s not technology; it’s not adherence to one way of making music. It’s about thinking about the connections between the people you’re working with. Saying ‘all of the above’ may be too easy an answer, but it does ascribe equal value to notation, improvisation and technology. These are all zones on the map and they all overlap each other, so the paths between those zones are what I’m interested in.”

***

Wright’s projects frequently overlap, the post production of one coinciding with the development of another. With summer approaching, Wright was mixing a duo session with Pat Thomas that has the flavor of This is Trickster; a Spheric Totemic album, and a Trance Map + recording on which Parker and him are joined by harpist Milana Zaric and Richard Barrett.

The presence of Barrett is particularly intriguing, as he pioneered improvised electronic music beginning in the 1990s – largely through FURT, his partnership with Paul Obermayer – laying groundwork for Wright and others. Additionally, Barrett’s compositions are renowned for testing – and often surpassing – the presumed physical limits of instrumentalists.

Barrett and Wright are part of a trajectory of composers foregrounding technology in their work. An earlier dot on the line, one that is essential but not obvious, is Conlon Nancarrow. The expatriate composer is the inspiration for Wright’s next major work, “Passing Nancarrow.” Wright’s latest project with the Belgian ensemble BL!NDMAN (the exclamation point is intentional) also has Hawkins in a key role. The piece debuts next year, marking 30 years since Nancarrow died.

“The idea of the piece is based around Nancarrow being obsessed with Art Tatum’s playing,” Wright explained. “He sampled Tatum in the form of piano rolls, using technology from a hundred years ago. What we will do is, while Alex improvises in real time, his notes are captured and this will trigger all sorts of reactions from the group. In a way, we turn Alex’s music into a piano roll.”

Wright was partly inspired by the writer and documentary film director Helen Borton’s comment that jazz and blues collide like a “hurricane” in Nancarrow’s music. Replace “hurricane” with “Nancarrow” and you get the gist of Wright’s conceptualization for the recording he is currently mixing – “four hurricanes of all kinds of crazy sounds.” Wright also considered the music of Squarepusher, Aphex Twin, and other exponents of electronic dance music, that influenced him when Nancarrow died in 1997, leading him to include “strange, intelligent dance music in the piece.”

However, the nexus of Nancarrow, Barrett, and Wright, is the consideration of the limits of music humans can create in real time, and how to get to the edge of those limits, if not extend them.

“Nancarrow reached for impossible, post-human music. But in my current work, I don’t have an artistic interest in post-human AI. I’ve heard a lot of AI-generated music and read a lot of AI research, and the thing I’m already bored by is that AI can do almost anything. Like a musician that can play everything and just won’t stop playing to give space for others, AI doing anything and everything is boring to me when you don’t hear inspired choices and you don’t hear the human labor or the human need for considered space in the music. But, I’m open minded. I just haven’t heard anything that inspires me yet. Back to the human level, in Alex’s piano playing, there is that reaching beyond what is supposedly humanly possible, to reach a new vista for what is possible.

“You can say that, for his times, Nancarrow was making a post-human kind of music, but we should remember that he sat there, punching holes. So, I don’t hear a sort of pre-AI in his music, a piano that can do anything, but the blood and the hours of Nancarrow sitting maybe six months to create an explosive two minutes. I want to know how humans feel when they hear music and when they make music. If that is aided by technology, the idea is that the technology helps musical thinking like an instrument helps musical thinking. My interest in technology is the same as Alex’s interest in the piano, there’s a tradition of human tool use there that in a sense heightens the human listening experience if done successfully.

“Another thing I like about Nancarrow was that he was true to his beliefs, which is why he left the US for Mexico City, which resulted in him working in relative isolation. He just got on with it. A few people had experimented with the player piano before, but he made it his own. I appreciate that you can hear the edges in music and you’re OK with not being able to know everything beyond that edge. I guess the difference between the scene we have now and Nancarrow’s situation is that we can go to the edge together in a collaborative spirit.”
