items.body: Summer is ending. We must not say this out loud; it is a hard pill to swallow. For many people, summer has already ended; vacations are over, classes have begun, the water has cooled. zakè‘s Tide Requiem for the Low Sea is a long, slow, poignant goodbye, holding on until the very last moment, like the last bit of a small island before it is submerged. The physical representation is gorgeous: a double-sided picture disc, suitable for framing, showcasing photography by Tom Meluch (Benoît Pioulard). The images inspired both the music and their titles. One can imagine clinging to one of these peaks, like Blake Lively in “The Shallows,” albeit with more sadness than drama. Each side contains a single track, logging in at 22:46. The title track occupies Side A, ebbing in and out like the tide. Precious piano notes float atop the layered, undulating drones. Time seems be in suspension, although this is an illusion; it is simply passing slowly and inexorably from summer to autumn. Larger chords pass like behemoths in the sea, never quite surfacing, as much a feeling as they are a presence. How long can one hold on before succumbing to the sea? The answer should be six hours, the distance between high and low tides, and while we are not requesting a six-hour recording, it would be interesting to experience. A quarter-day at the beach allows for nuance, for incremental change that eventually grows extreme. “Tide Requiem for the Low Sea” seems to reflect the ocean at its lowest, before the rising tide, when one is aware that time is limited. The complementary “Crimson Covenant” is like a different viewpoint of a similar scene or like two persons comparing notes. Is the tide advancing or receding, and is the glass half full or half empty? If there is value to be found in each, might it also be applied to the changing seasons? The chords are darker, as one might expect from the title, which (likely coincidentally) is shared with an RPG. They advance and recede more swiftly, like the reduced interval between waves. The organ-like tones contribute elegance and gravity. Funeral offers music as a bridge between worlds; this piece suggests a similar metaphor. One of the unique curiosities of the record (as opposed to the download) is that the needle grows ever closer to an island peak, beginning at the outskirts as it alternately treads water and rests on land. The implication is that even the needle is seeking safety from the tide, and eventually finds it. The same may be true for the listener, leaving the seas of summer and landing safely on the shores of fall. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: drone / ambient / contemporary classical / modern composition
items._cn_summary: zakè 的《Tide Requiem for the Low Sea》以双面黑胶形式发行，每面收录一首近 23 分钟的长篇作品。Tom Meluch 的摄影作品同时启发了音乐与曲名，画面与声响彼此呼应。A 面标题曲以缓慢起伏的低音 drone 为底，钢琴音符漂浮其上，巨大的和弦如海中巨兽般在深处游动却不曾浮出水面，整体呈现潮水将退未退的悬停感。B 面《Crimson Covenant》色调更暗，管风琴般的音色带来庄严与重量，音潮进出更为急促。黑胶唱针从外围逐渐靠近画面中央的岛屿峰顶，象征聆听者从夏日之海安全抵达秋季之岸。整张专辑围绕季节更迭与潮汐隐喻展开，将物理媒介、视觉影像与缓慢展开的氛围音乐融合为统一的艺术整体。

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — "Ys", named for the mythical and unfairly sunken Breton kingdom, isn't JOANNA NEWSOM channeling early Breton harpist Alan Stivell (who, like all good Bretons, reveres Ys"), and it isn't reimagining "The Milk Eyed Mender" in broad and long strokes, though simplistically that isn't utterly false. Its 5 tracks are not just epic in their length but in their subject matter and classically oriented arrangements deliberately drumkit deprived, the themes of family ties, co-dependency, love, aging and loss permeate the lyrics far better than the lyrics themselves permeate the consciousness. given her impossibly odd and arguably miraculous accent and phrasings. The subconscious, well that's another matter. I'm still processing, I think.Most of these works are afforded space in the early going, eventually accelerating into a breathless stream of consciousness, as impossible as this sounds. She is too unpolished to be rehearsed, and too polished to be unrehearsed, while similar could be said of the orchestral flourishes throughout, which seem to interject themselves desperately during the few 10-20 seconds interludes where she is presumably recouping respiratory capacity. Nothing here is weak but I especially the first for its lucid melody and the last for its approximation of a Baptist cum shaker hymn ("How can I keep from singing") through the lens of the American southeast. Don't expect to be grabbed and held from the outset. "Ys" requires a shedding of all your musical instincts to prejudge, judge, and judge some more after what should be enough devoted time, but its lyrical and musical messages preach patience and ruminations on aspects of life and lore over which sensitive folk have pored since music preceded language. It's not going to help our neuroses but it does, in a most whimsically idiosyncratic way, assure us we are not the only ones trying to make sense of it all.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以布列塔尼传说中沉没的王国命名，五首曲目篇幅极为宏大，主题围绕家庭纽带、依赖关系、爱、衰老与丧失展开。乔安娜·纽瑟姆以竖琴为核心乐器，配以管弦乐编排，刻意去除鼓组配置，营造出古典倾向的氛围。她独特的发音与断句方式使歌词难以直接理解，却能渗透潜意识。多数作品以舒缓空间展开，随后加速为密集的意识流。管弦乐段落在她换气的间隙中急切地介入。评论者尤其推荐第一首的清晰旋律与最后一首对美国南方浸信会赞美诗的致敬。整张专辑需要听众放下预判的习惯，以耐心与沉思的姿态进入，在音乐的反复咀嚼中感受其对生命与传说的独特诠释。

items.body: The Axiom Divide begins with a grand premise: a doorway to hidden knowledge, an Egyptian afterlife reimagined as a psychological chamber where curiosity becomes a kind of initiation. On The Halls of Amenti: Remixes, that premise is handed to seven other producers and projects, each asked to rebuild the same architecture from a different angle. The result is a remix collection with enough stylistic range to work in a club while preserving the philosophical charge at the center of the original. Jay Tye and Brent Heinze make an effective pairing because their histories already suggest two sides of the project. Tye, known for Soil & Eclipse, brings the gothic gravity and vocal drama; Heinze, whose work includes Probe 7 and the revived Darling Kandie with Franke “Groovie Mann” Nardiello, supplies a producer’s instinct for structure, movement, and electronic detail. Together, they push darkwave and futurepop toward something theatrical, with operatic and choral ideas hovering over machinery built for physical response. The remixers have plenty of material to dismantle. Razed in Black, Pygmy Children, Frontal Boundary, Fermion, I Am Consumer, and Dread Risks approach the source from separate corners of the dark electronic spectrum, turning the EP into a broad survey rather than a stack of minor variations. The sequencing helps: repeated encounters with The Halls of Amenti begin to resemble successive chambers, each version changing the perceived dimensions of the same symbolic room. Across the collection, solemnity and propulsion remain in productive tension, with melody acting as the connective thread. Repetition becomes conceptual, each mix opening another passage through a chamber the listener already recognizes and understands. The band explains the concept directly: “The symbolism behind…The Halls of Amenti references Egyptian lore to describe a metaphorical spiritual realm where a repository of forgotten knowledge welcomes an individual’s search for enlightenment,” says the band. “When the seeker of truth is deemed worthy, they are granted entry into this space to expand their mind and spirit. It speaks to our search for wisdom and personal discovery to enrich our lives.” That language could easily collapse under its own metaphysical density, yet the remix format keeps the record moving. Ideas of enlightenment, forgotten knowledge, and spiritual worthiness are translated into tempo, repetition, pressure, and release. Closing with Probe 7’s remix of Unrequited is a smart choice because it breaks the recursive spell of the title track and gives Heinze a final opportunity to refract The Axiom Divide through one of his own established identities. As an introduction to the project, The Halls of Amenti: Remixes presents Tye and Heinze as musicians interested in philosophy without sacrificing the body, treating the dance floor as another possible doorway into altered perception. Listen to The Halls Of Amenti: Remixes below and order the album here. items.body: After the brutal heatwaves of August, the chilly depths of winter feel like a distant threat. But signs of the creeping cold are slowly emerging; cooling nights, the return of pumpkin spice, a dwindling tomato season. For those ready for the crisp return of colder weather, there’s Convulsif’s latest album, which is slowly unfolding like the change of seasons. Today, a new glimpse is unveiled. Fittingly, “A Torch Then Blaze” is something of a transitional track on Anatomy of Rage. A quick, bass-heavy interlude that emerges with sinister intent and lurching grooves spliced with grinding noise that connects the blistering first chapter with the funeral pyres of the middle tracks.While short, “A Torch Then Blaze” illustrates the fascinating juxtapositions created by Convulsif: maximalist experiments constrained within minimalist production, chaotic noise rock sharpened to a razor’s edge. Rather than embrace the massive production often found in experimental rock, Convulsif keeps their sound centered and brutally direct. Structure loses all meaning - songs range from 76 seconds to nearly 20 minutes - allowing tightly coiled grooves and jagged, jazzy rhythms to take control. The clarity creates a menacing beast of noise and abrasion, one that’s encapsulated by the brief warning siren of “A Torch Then Blaze” as it groans and explodes into noisy flames. Anatomy of Rage will be released on October 1, 2026. Pre-order on Bandcamp and follow the band via their website.
items._genre: noise rock / experimental / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 本文是瑞士乐队Convulsif即将发行的专辑《Anatomy of Rage》的单曲首发表。文章以季节更替的隐喻开篇，详细介绍了过渡性曲目《A Torch Then Blaze》：这是一首短暂、以贝斯为主导的插曲，在刺耳的碾核噪音与阴森的低音律动之间切换，承担着连接专辑开头与中段葬礼般氛围的桥梁功能。乐评着重指出乐队的核心美学张力——在极简的制作框架中嵌入最大化实验，混乱的噪音摇滚被打磨成锋利的刀刃。歌曲结构在此变得无关紧要，时长从76秒到近20分钟不等，紧绷的律动和棱角分明的爵士节奏获得主导权，由此诞生出一种兼具威胁感与清晰度的噪音猛兽。整体评介强调了乐队拒绝实验摇滚常见的宏大制作、选择保持声音居中且直接暴烈的路线。

items.body:
1970 (April 10th, 1970 – IBC Studios, London)

Negotiations were now underway between Sean Murphy and several labels including Deram, CBS and Harvest, the EMI sub-label that had distributed Volume Two in the UK and already had Kevin Ayers in its stable. “They are still not an attraction in the very top bracket, so it was a pleasant surprise to see major companies throwing in genuinely massive bids earlier this year when the group was looking for a recording deal,” Richard Williams revealed. Ultimately, Soft Machine signed with CBS, but Third was self-financed, taken partly from studio sessions, but also from live recordings (“Facelift”) and edits and loops of tapes made by Mike Ratledge and Hugh Hopper at the home of Bob Woolford, who had let them use his Brenell and Stellavox tape recorders. Such infringements of accepted professional practices were only possible because CBS, having acquired a finished album, were no longer in a position to force the band to comply with them.

The benefit for Soft Machine in terms of artistic freedom is easy to measure. But this has to be balanced against the fact that the production on Third is, to put it bluntly, an unmitigated disaster. IBC, at the time the studio of choice for such notorious perfectionists as The Who and the Bee Gees, are probably less to blame than the band themselves who, in spite of the issues with Volume Two, are again credited as sole producers. The sound suffers from almost constantly saturated low frequencies and extremely vague mediums, the drums are much too low in the mix, as if played behind a closed door; and the organ is deprived of much of its biting impact through overwhelming equalization. Unfortunately the 2007 remaster, while an improvement, fails to rectify this.

What is problematic is that, as well as making the album an uncomfortable listen, its sub-par production lessens the claim, widely held at the time of its release, that Third represented musical state-of-the-art. This claim was based on Soft Machine’s ability, unparalleled among their contemporaries, to draw from and amalgamate an exceptionally wide range of influences. Starting out as a rock band, and then gradually moving towards jazz to invent a uniquely personal, and absolutely valid, British answer to American fusion, Soft Machine went even further, incorporating the influence of Stockhausen’s avant-garde and Terry Riley’s repetitive minimalism. Third’s ‘total’ vision, encompassing the entire spectrum of known musical genres, placed Soft Machine at the forefront of musical “progress” in 1970. However, horizons have since expanded to such an extent, beyond the Western tradition in particular, that this concept of universality has aged considerably.

In his insightful review of Third for Actuel, Paul Alessandrini wrote of “music to really listen to, no longer aiming for a purely physical vibration, more interiorized. Soft Machine have re-thought their musical influences – Riley, Cecil Taylor, Coltrane – to really make them their own, abandoning their aesthetics of random explosion in favor of a much more thought-out approach.” There are still occasional reminders of these sonic excesses that, as Alessandrini noted, had now largely disappeared from their music. Mike Ratledge's lengthy solo introduction to “Facelift” almost sounds like an electric exorcism, as if to rid Soft Machine of what still remains of that violence in order to reinvent their music in a more controlled manner, setting formal perfection as their new objective.

Considered as a whole, Hugh Hopper's piece represents the last remnant of Soft Machine’s early days, when they still favored spirit over form - here found lacking in both sound quality and performance, with a few train wrecks along the way - and were intent on disregarding the accepted rules. “Facelift” includes free sections increasingly at odds with Ratledge’s preoccupation with structure – and while as a keyboard player, he still embodies the band’s more radical leanings, Ratledge’s own compositions reveal a much less iconoclastic temperament. Hopper described his own approach at the time as “halfway between” that of Dean, “whose thing is really total improvisation, without any structure, and on the other extreme, [that of Ratledge] who's into entirely formalized musical forms.

“Moon in June” completes Robert Wyatt’s donation to Soft Machine of the material originally intended for his first solo album in 1968. It is interesting to note that Wyatt does this at the exact point where Soft Machine had shed any remaining reference to pop in their live repertoire. Looking back, Wyatt was certainly justified in saying that his side of Third was “the last chance I had to use all the things we'd done without being a jazz band. I wanted to get twenty minutes of it down somewhere.” And since his colleagues, reluctant to act as mere accompanists, had made no secret of their lack of interest in his songs, he recorded most of “Moon in June” on his own, repeating the modus operandi of the 1968-69 demo. Hugh Hopper and Mike Ratledge’s participation is again limited to the organ solo halfway through (Hopper also plays a short melodic theme earlier in the piece). Elton Dean wasn’t asked to contribute anything – Wyatt’s unconvincing justification being that he “hadn’t yet worked out how to work on [his] stuff with the added wind instruments.”

As there was no mention of this breach of band discipline in the sleeve notes, only the most astute listeners noticed that the organ heard during the first ten minutes was a Hammond rather than Ratledge’s signature Lowrey, that the playing clearly wasn’t Ratledge’s, and that most of the ‘bass’ parts were played on an electric piano. When the truth was finally revealed, Wyatt gave contradictory versions of what had happened – in one interview claiming that Ratledge and Hopper had “refused to play [on “Moon in June”] and I had to play it all myself,” in another that he’d “almost had to force them to get them to play on it, which I thought was rather unfair as I’d done my best to get into the music they were writing.” Probably the most objective and believable of Wyatt’s rationales was that he was “terrified it’d be played wrong” if he didn’t perform it all himself.

To approach “Moon in June” as a ‘message’ song would misrepresent Wyatt’s more mundane intent, insofar as the phonetic qualities of the words often seem to matter more to him than their meaning. In other words, “Moon in June” is above all a musical composition, a suite of instrumental sections, some of which are adorned with melodies and lyrics, and others not. The singing accompanies the music rather than vice-versa. In this respect, outside of a possible rivalry with Elton Dean and Wyatt’s inability to sing while drumming, there was no theoretical incompatibility between Soft Machine’s move towards jazz and the continued presence of Wyatt’s voice (even if limited to the Echoplexed scat singing of his solitary interludes during the band’s concerts). Dispensing with vocals was the single most questionable move in Soft Machine’s entire musical evolution, not to mention one whose commercial consequences cannot be underestimated. In different circumstances, Hugh Hopper would surely have joined Wyatt in lobbying for having at least some vocals, but in addition to his increasingly strained personal relationship with Wyatt, Hopper had at this point completely lost interest in non-instrumental music. “I find that using the human voice means asserting limitations to your music right from the start”, he explained in 1972. “I am more interested in the sounds generated by instruments, or electronic devices, because the possibilities offered by songs are much more limited than when experimenting with sounds.”

Even if there was no future for singing in Soft Machine, “Moon in June” at least offers evidence that Robert Wyatt, in a voice-free context, could still be more than “a session drummer for an interesting new species of jazz groups,” as long as he contributed to the writing. When it came to extended pieces, he could stand comparison with Mike Ratledge, even though he lacked any comparable academic background. In addition to its constant melodic inspiration, “Moon in June” is very skillfully constructed (indeed, its instrumental architecture had remained intact since 1968), and confirms Wyatt’s seemingly innate talent for making a coherent whole out of ill-assorted musical ideas.

items._cn_summary: 本文评述Soft Machine第三张专辑的创作背景与制作过程。乐队与CBS签约后获得前所未有的创作自由，自筹资金完成专辑，录音素材来自工作室、演出实况以及成员在家用磁带机上进行的编辑与循环实验。文章批评专辑混音质量低劣，低频饱和、中频模糊、鼓声被掩埋、失去冲击力，使这张曾被视为音乐前沿代表的作品听起来极为不适。乐评指出，专辑的真正价值在于其试图融合爵士、摇滚、Stockhausen的先锋派与Terry Riley的简约重复音乐等多元影响，构建了一种涵盖已知音乐光谱的"总体"视野，创造了融合美国爵士的英式回应。然而作者认为，随着西方传统之外的视野不断扩展，这种普世性概念已显陈旧。整体而言，文章聚焦于制作困境与跨流派融合的雄心之间的张力。

items.body: Slow Reels is a record of love. Ian Hawgood’s passion for reel-to-reel tape machines and vintage synths combines with James Murray’s love for strong melodicism and deep textures. Farewell Islands drifts over sustained, sleeping drones and hazy ambient atmospheres which are evocative of the great outdoors, ascending like smoke over a forest. The pair have released one another’s music on their own respective labels, Home Normal and Slowcraft, but their musical collaboration only recently began. While Hawgood was living in Warsaw, he spent long nights with his collection of reel-to-reel machines, pouring over the sound and the special tone it produces; the magic sound. Broken things – both instruments and people – produce special, heartfelt music, it seems. Music that, in its own way, is eternal; magic music. “I created a number of loops with an old and sadly dying Akai which was noisy and would stutter quite a bit. I also found myself using older tape on cracked reels and the effects of this really helped develop a newer path for my own work”. In London, Murray added piano, guitar, and synthesizers, helping to form the haunting atmosphere. The record also recalls a fragile ambient, similar to the kind found in Japan, largely due to the thinner, delicate nature of its texture and the infinite depth of tape. Nothing else can really match that – not even the pristine, bordering on sterile digital format (although it’s worth pointing out that the record wouldn’t exist without digital technology). The older technology gives the music something of an older feel: decades old, removed from this century, even, recessed into the past. The music mirrors this feeling of the old gradually becoming older. As looping echoes continue to cycle with thin, vaporous breaths, they travel on, coming from an ancient place but also seemingly eternal. Clinks and vague clicks are left to form like gathering dust, falling upon the record’s surface. The same dust falls upon the reels. Shimmering, romantic tones offer lovely textures which fold over the surroundings. Farewell Islands is a record of transparency, but it’s also one of surprises. The clear tones are sometimes anchored by heavier tones, rumbling like distant thunder among the music’s other elemental forces, and although some tones are as light as air, Slow Reels manages to display an impressive tonal density. These islands are “places of meaning to both of us in our lives, found now only out of time…out of reach”. www.morrmusic.com
items._genre: ambient / drone / tape music / experimental electronic
items._cn_summary: 《Slow Reels》是Ian Hawgood与James Murray以Farewell Islands名义合作的首张专辑，核心围绕开盘磁带与复古合成器的质感展开。Hawgood在华沙的深夜里使用濒临报废的Akai设备、带有裂痕的旧磁带进行循环录制，刻意保留机器的噪音、卡顿与衰退痕迹，使录音本身带有时间磨损的纹理。Murray在伦敦叠加钢琴、吉他与合成器，以稀疏的旋律线条与绵延的低频铺底构建氛围。整体音色稀薄、朦胧，呼应日本式空灵氛围的美学取向，循环回声如远古气息般循环往复。轻盈的高频泛音与远处雷鸣般的低频共振并存，磁带特有的温暖失真赋予音乐一种超越当下的时间感。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑汇编了圣多美和普林西比1970至80年代的Puxa音乐，是该系列第二卷。Puxa是一种融合多种元素的复合节奏，吸收了前葡萄牙非洲殖民地音乐养分，并混入merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等律动，其舞蹈传统据说可召灵或驱魔，葡萄牙殖民者曾试图禁止却未能成功。评论指出，尽管圣多美是非洲第二小国、音乐场景有限，但这些录音展现了岛屿独有的声音特质。专辑收录15首作品，多把吉他交织盘旋，主唱与和声相互呼应，形成旋律框架。Pedro Lima领衔的乐队在《Sossegado》中以闷音吉他与鼓组对峙；Sangazuza在低音与键盘退出后让鼓与吉他驱动舞者；Africa Negra的曲目则呈现了现场可能持续数小时的延伸律动。这批录音提供了关于一个鲜少被记录的小岛音乐文化的珍贵窗口。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了贝宁传奇乐队Orchestre Poly-Rythmo与创作人Antoine Dougbé在1977至1982年间合作的作品。Dougbé以击打腿部制造Cavacha节奏而闻名，他将源自鼓手Meridjo从火车节奏中提炼的律动带入创作，其音乐深深植根于伏都教传统。他被称为"魔鬼首相"，只与Poly-Rythmo合作，因他认为唯有该乐队能准确呈现其构想。乐评指出，由于录音年代跨越七十年代末到八十年代初，作品音色有明显演变——吉他呈现出塑料般的光泽感，合成器开始登场，但根基仍稳固在七十年代的律动之上。古巴son风格的影响在专辑开篇尤为明显，合成器铺垫的曲目中，闪亮的高帽律动配合紧绷吉他线条层层推进；而另一首作品则更具古巴风格，以持续牛铃、经典鼻音对唱和紧密重复的吉他乐句构建出浓郁的跨大西洋对话。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._genre: world fusion / experimental / klezmer / cumbia / afrobeat
items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的这张专辑延续了首作的风格杂烩，最大特色在于所有演奏乐器均由废弃杂物手工自制，诸如厨房号角、克拉里坚果管等。在这些自造乐器上，乐队成功呈现了克莱兹默、昆比亚、桑巴、非洲节拍及中东风格等多种世界音乐的融合。评论指出这些自制乐器在音准和录音质量上表现出色，完全不逊于商业乐器。曲目中常融入即兴段落，展现出演奏者扎实的音乐功底，乐句常以爵士化的切分方式游离于节拍之外。从这些作品中可以感受到跨文化音乐的活力，以及音乐家利用有限资源创造声音的巧思，专辑传递出音乐作为一种普世情感表达的核心价值。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这是挪威Camilla Hole Trio继前作探索科幻合成器与传统素材结合之后的最新专辑，相较前作更回归本土。专辑以高音萨克斯为核心，融入爵士即兴语汇，同时与挪威西部民间舞曲素材交织。三人组合中乐手角色并不固定，节奏组与旋律线条不断互换位置，贝斯手和鼓手随时拿起主奏乐器展开即兴对话。开场曲目以民间旋律起手，随后通过模块合成器与颤音琴的叠加逐步扩展音色层次，作品在结构松散中保持着即兴张力。整体呈现一种将北欧民俗、爵士自由演奏与电子音色相互渗透的跨界美学。

items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?

items._cn_summary: 这是丹麦三人组合 GuldGanger 的首张数字 EP，由北欧民谣圈资深歌手 Mia Guldhammer 领衔。五首作品以传统素材为主，成员各自带入不同视角。开场曲《Svennedal》以粗犷奔腾的节奏展示主唱极具说服力的嗓音；《Nordgård》是乐队成员 Morten Musicus 的唯一原创，口琴与风笛带来持续推进感；传统曲目《Agnete Of Bjergmanden》以扬琴做细腻底色；终曲《Orms》作为器乐曲，由口琴、长笛与弦乐交织，呈现出不安分却令人振奋的气质。整体弥漫着古老、略带吱呀感的氛围，虽仅是五首短篇，却展现出乐队成熟的整体素养，为后续完整专辑埋下期待。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由瑞典小提琴手与两位挪威乐手组成三重奏，演奏源自斯堪的纳维亚的传统舞曲素材，但以极度非传统的方式重新诠释。乐评将其比作室内乐——三位乐手沉浸在亲密的音乐对话中，剥离了舞曲原本的伴舞功能，转而探索音乐内部隐藏的意义层面与暗流。Tellef Kvifte 主要以竖笛领奏旋律，辅以萨克斯和风笛等挪威传统之外的乐器；Knut Kvifte Nesheim 的打击乐则模糊了不同音乐类型之间的界限。专辑以挪威 Setesdal 地区的"Fossgrimen"开场，这个与瀑布精灵相关的传说暗示了民间音乐中深层的魔力与不安。在"Polska from Per Myhr"等曲目中，传统的旋律线条在引入后迅速碎裂、瓦解，呈现出解构与即兴的特质。整体而言，这是一张介于北欧民俗、实验即兴与现代室内乐之间的跨界作品，揭示了舞曲表层欢愉之下潜藏的阴暗张力。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴音乐厅完成了一张独奏即兴作品。疫情期间他在空荡的音乐厅内对 Fazioli 大三角钢琴进行两小时无脚本即兴演奏，后期混入少量人声采样、打击乐、循环声、实地录音和拾得音效。Sosa 师承 Monk 的理念，从不重复同一首作品，强调首遍录音的自然直觉和'less is more'的美学。他的创作拒绝被归入爵士、拉丁、timba、雷鬼顿或古典等任何风格范畴，而是将所有影响以全新方式融合，并保留与低脉轮共鸣的传统音乐泛音。文章以专辑开篇曲为例，展现他用指尖拨弄琴弦激发钢琴本体共鸣、随后叠加轻量打击的创作手法。

items.body: Toronto-based duo Kazdoura debuted their single “Taa” on COLORS, taking their Levantine psych-rock to the platform’s bare monochrome stage. for a stripped set putting the song’s guitar and voice fully in view. The track opens on intricate guitar motifs over an ominous chord progression, before a steady drum groove settles underneath. Leen Hamo‘s vocal carries the phrasing of vintage Arabic pop, floating over the arrangement as it tightens through the verses and opens into a chorus built on a hypnotic, ride-cymbal-led rhythm. Hamo, who is Syrian, and Lebanese multi-instrumentalist John Abou Chacra formed Kazdoura in Toronto. The name means “to stroll” in Levantine Arabic, and the JUNO Award-winning duo draw on Arabic maqam melodies while layering in psychedelic soul, jazz and funk. The lyrics deal with memory and the difficulty of letting go. The COLORS premiere opens a European run that starts at Spillestedet Stengade in Copenhagen on August 28 and the Habibi Funk Festival in London on August 29 and 30. From there the duo plays the Jam Jar in Bristol on September 3, Norwich Arts Centre on September 4, Peggy’s Skylight in Nottingham on September 6, and a show in Istanbul on September 11, before Paradiso in Amsterdam on September 15 and the Reeperbahn Festival in Hamburg on September 17 and 18. Stream “Taa” HERE and get your copy of their debut album Ghoyoum غيوم following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Kazdoura – Taa | A COLORS SHOW appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Northern Earth is a fully instrumental, sprawling and contemplative sound journey of minimalist, solitary-mood pieces which deserve patience and spiritual disposition. Mystical devotion and cinematic splendor Northern Earth by Dean McPhee   Dean McPhee is a sound artist and a guitarist apart from restricted stylistic categories. His musical production spans more than a decade with steady releases on some obscure indie labels. His last efforts have been released under his own publishing structure: Bass Ritual. Released in 2011, his album for Blast First Petite (owned by Paul Smith of Mute) is unfortunately the only one I got familiar with, but I will definitely try to correct this lack of knowledge. Comparing this older work with the new offer, we might say that McPhee rapidly found his musical path back then, mixing with skills, spirit and evocativeness a chilling emotional psychedelic folk mantra with hypnotic looped effects obtained with guitars. Northern Earth follows a relatively similar path, with an emphasis on repetitive and ritualized guitar-centered soundscapes of heavenly and spiritual beauty behind more raw textured motifs. In a way, it reminds me of lonesome krautrockin’ excursions from the 70s with Popol Vuh, Ash Ra Tempel, or even Fripp/Eno lyergic grooves (in the self-titled track), but here the whole thing embraces a sense of existential wandering, natural vastness, mystical devotion and cinematic splendor. Rolling percussive pulses and nuanced effects :: The guitar is generally soaked in a heavy pack of reverbs, also turning on slightly relaxing slide style, alternating sinuous textures with moody-esque repetitive melodies that will lead you in a beatific state. Rare sound objects, rolling percussive pulses and nuanced effects punctuate the body of tracks. I must say it is a welcoming surprise and a break from the too ambient-ish electronic efforts I reviewed recently. Absolutely recommended for fans of Cosmic Americana (as a musical subgenre), Pan•American, Stars of the Lid, Labradford, Saadé. It would have made a nice soundtrack for some road movies and slow-moving western-themed films by Jim Jarmusch or Kelly Reichardt in Meek’s Cutoff’ Northern Earth is a fully instrumental, sprawling and contemplative sound journey of minimalist, solitary-mood pieces which deserve patience and spiritual disposition. Northern Earth is available on Bass Ritual. [Bandcamp] Northern Earth by Dean McPheeThe post Dean McPhee :: Northern Earth (Bass Ritual) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by HogweedOfTuscany — aka "the most irresistible album I've ever hated."The story of Marillion and their transformation is something that doesn't need any further explanations or elaborations ... not in 2026, at least. It took me a long, very long time to fall in love in their "latter" era (which easily dwarfs their early era by now, whether in years or in albums, and can be therefore quite safely considered their "main" or "primary" era by even the most rabid Fish aficionados) and to be perfectly honest, Brave can be at least partially blamed for that.As a friend of mine had put it once, "Brave is what Marillion sounds like to people who hate Marillion" and I can't stop thinking about that. Brave has the iconic album cover, the iconic concept, the reputation of being one of the Hogarth-era Marillion's undisputable highlights - it could be arguably considered the most famous oeuvre of the Fishless band. And it is also a dour, brooding, static, soft and quiet, melodyless dirge that would put a chainsaw to sleep. And no, although I love the album now, after years of being obsessed with it despite hating it, I won't mince my words. Brave may be - for all its unassuming qualities and the almost mainstream sound - one of the most unwelcoming albums I have ever heard, comparable to Trout Mask Replica, even. At first, it's just a drone - so post-rockish that it becomes almost half-ambient, slow, quiet and absolutely unmemorable. There are songs that completely lack discernible structure (and opening the album with one of them - Living with the Big Lie - is certainly an artistic choice) and even those that are lively and could be almost considered catchy (Lap of Luxury, Paper Lies and Hard as Love, which all sounds like the band has been provided a rejuvenated bolt of cocaine as if Fish wandered back into the studio to greet old friends and forget some powder behind) are mercilessly sabotaged by the production, which is so tinny and weak that the songs just do not work that way. I won't lie to you, after three listens, pretty much all I could remember from this 70+ minute album was: A. hogarth's histrionics as he shouts the title very near the end of Living with the Big Lie, B. that Rothery's wistful, almost pastoral guitar part on Runaway, C. Lap of Luxury chorus, D. "Baby, nothing else has ever been as hard as love", E. the bagpipes on the title track. The rest was all a mush and a definite proof that Marillion have finally metamorphosed into a fully post-rock ensemble, deciding that everything should be subjugated to the amoebous, indifferent cruel mistress called "atmosphere". I hated the album.And yet, I came back. Not that I would necessarily remember that much more with repeated listens and not that I would particularly enjoy the bleak mood of the album (I like me some melancholy, sure, but it has to be meaningful melancholy), but somehow I couldn't stay away. Brave became the dragon I had to slay, in order to appreciate Harillion and understand why the fans are so obsessed they travel half the globe to watch them perform this in full on a Marillion weekend, or why their fanclub releases are so bizarrely numerous. Every few months or so, I'd put this weird album with the weird blurred bird on the cover and the indecipherable themes - starting with the album title - and I was obsessed with how I didn't get it. I don't know when it clicked for me. In fact, I'm not even sure IF it clicked for me, or if I've just somehow abused my mind so as to embrace the album like a true contrarian. The album is like the river Severn, really. You see a tiny single wave that you like, but you can't really identify it, you can't keep watching it; it will disappear out of sight. It's a mass, a flow, a churning, but really unchanging, unthinking volume of water. You can call the river stupid, but it will be there once you've been gone. The only thing that remains is the option to consider drowning yourself in it, as so many have before. And be called Brave by Hogarth for that consideration. I don't know what to say about this album, my musical words fail me. I think I love it, but I don't know why. However, don't give up, when all is said and done, it's pretty cool. Hypnotic, even. If you wish to get into hogarth-era Marillion, though, maybe go for a different album first, like Marbles.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以阴郁、缓慢的氛围铺陈为主，结构松散，旋律不显著，大量依赖静态音色与情绪张力构建。评论者描述其听感接近半氛围化的后摇滚，缺乏清晰可辨的歌曲框架，部分曲目虽有较强旋律性却被薄弱制作所拖累。专辑以概念为核心，整体气质沉重而疏离，对于偏好实验、氛围与跨界融合的听众而言，其后摇滚与氛围化的走向具有一定吸引力，但歌曲结构上的模糊与制作上的不足使其难以完全满足对创新性和融合度的期待。评论文字虽未完结，但已提供较丰富的音乐质感描述。

items.body: (Colin Currie Group perform Steve Reich’s Quartet) Steve Reich’s ninetieth anniversary year would not be complete without a world premiere. Or two, as was the case in this evening’s all-Reich concert at Usher Hall, Edinburgh. There again, a Reich premiere would not be complete without the Colin Curry Group either, with Quartet (also on the programme) and Traveler’s Prayer previous co-commissions for Currie’s group. Forming part of this year’s Edinburgh International Festival, these two new compositions – Two Pianos and the stirring, spectacular In All Your Ways – appeared in either half of the program. More on that later. The evening began with Clapping Music, probably Reich’s most performed piece. Currie performed the piece on several occasions with Reich himself and recently told me that the experience was, in his words: ‘Completely surreal, yet not at all nerve-wrecking. Reich was a great person to take to the stage with, and I miss that interaction. I’m so glad I had that opportunity to perform with him.’ Certainly, fellow percussionist Owen Gunnell acquitted himself to the task at the Usher Hall’s reverberant acoustics, the duet executing the piece’s gradually shifting patterns with consummate ease. This was followed by the first of two premieres. Two Pianos was originally composed by Reich in 2020, but for various reasons (the Pandemic amongst them) was held back until this year. Chorale-like in scope, the stately, slow-moving four-minute work revolved around a series of imposing harmonic pillars whose true significance was only completely revealed at the end. Thereafter, the program took an upturn in energy and pace. The opening movement of the Radiohead-inspired Radio Rewrite for ensemble gained much from the way in which Currie – now conducting – managed to bind together its complex movable parts, his ensemble always alert to the music’s sudden shifts and tricky corners. The performance also managed to set the music’s propulsive qualities very effectively against more plangent moments heard during the second and fourth sections, while the closing movement rocked and rolled with more swagger and conviction than the Bon Jovi concert taking place down the road at the Murrayfield Stadium the same evening. Double Sextet provided a virtuosic end to the first half, with the first movement surging out of the blocks like a tearaway train and the third movement forever straining at the leash. The second half began much as the first had ended, this time with Quartet, pianists Philip Moore and Siwan Rhys and percussionists Currie and Gunnell locked tightly together throughout, sculpting the music’s peaks and troughs with power, accuracy, and precision. And so, to the evening’s highlight: Reich’s new work In All Your Ways. Scored for three sets of quartets (comprising woodwinds, percussion and strings), plus two pianos, the title is taken from Proverbs 3:6: ‘In all your ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct your paths.’ About as far removed from the composer’s recent Traveler’s Prayer as one could imagine, In All Your Ways was a revelation: Reich rethought and rewrought. Teeming with cascades of rising and falling lines that followed each other with almost breathless virtuosity and abandon, In All your Ways was far more linear in scope than what we have come to expect from this composer. Reich will often combine lines and layers vertically rather than horizontally. Once a rhythmic pattern is stated and its harmonic foundations in place, he will then present and develop the material by gradually introducing interlocking lines and close canons above them. Reich’s musical conception is often therefore ‘simultaneous’ rather than ‘successive’, with patterns appearing as subdivisions of the beat. In All Your Ways turns that idea on its head. These rhythmic subdivisions result in ever-shifting and ever-changing kaleidoscopic colours – a dizzying sequence of melodic spirals, often played in unison rather than utilizing the composer’s trademark close canons. Alongside these uplifting moments, the middle section contained tender lyrical passages that appeared to draw inspiration from the melodic character of Reich’s opera The Cave. A beautiful moment appeared towards the end of the work as well, where time appeared to stand still. Reich has noted that In All Your Ways is based on four rhythmic sections (sixteenths, eighths, quarters, triplets) alongside four harmonic areas, but the impression was of something more fluid, integrated, and organic. One cannot draw too many conclusions from one performance, of course, but In All Your Ways is a powerhouse of a piece that ranks alongside some of the composer’s other late masterpieces, such as Runner and Reich/Richter. If you missed the premiere, Colin Currie Group will also be performing In All Your Ways at the Concertgebouw, Amsterdam on 19 September; Barbican, London on 28 October; Philharmonie, Paris on 22 November; and Großer Saal, Hamburg on 4 December; with Canadian and US premieres given by Soundstreams Canada and Ensemble Signal, Bang on a Can All-Stars and Brad Lubman, on 6 & 22 October respectively. Not to be missed! The post Colin Currie Group Plays Steve Reich (Edinburgh International Festival, 28 August 2026) appeared first on Sequenza21.

items._cn_summary: 本文记录了Colin Currie Group在爱丁堡国际艺术节上演奏Steve Reich作品的专场音乐会。正值Reich九十寿辰，音乐会上演了两首新作的世界首演：原为2020年创作的《Two Pianos》以及取材自《圣经·箴言》的《In All Your Ways》，后者以三组四重奏加两架钢琴编制呈现。上半场还包括拍手节奏作品《Clapping Music》、受Radiohead启发的《Radio Rewrite》以及《Double Sextet》，下半场则以弦乐四重奏与打击乐的对话《Quartet》收束。Currie在指挥与打击乐之间切换，乐队对Reich标志性的相位偏移技法与脉冲节奏结构展现出精确的控制力。乐评侧重于对演出细节与现场音响效果的描述，而非音乐学层面的深度剖析。

items.body: Wrote my Senator, “Senator, what can you do?” But my dear Senator, you sold your soul to AIPAC too. There is something painfully American in the picture Stephen Bluhm draws in Emotional Plea: a man seated before a screen, writing senators, sending money, updating a résumé, scrolling through reports of strangers killed under another sky, while beneath these acts of conscience a disco beat keeps immaculate time. The first single from Work Crush, Bluhm’s quirky new project, takes political despair out of the arena of slogans and places it in the room where most people encounter it, alone with a telephone, a computer, a paycheck, and the knowledge that private life has become entangled with public cruelty. Bluhm, a longtime figure in New York’s Hudson Valley music community, gives that unease an unexpectedly elegant body. Recorded with Alex Wernquest at Basement Floods in Catskill, the song advances on a firm dance rhythm while synthesizers and clipped, Nile Rodgers-like guitar strokes gather around it. Mike Watt, the Minutemen co-founder whose bass playing carries muscle and wit, moves melodically through the track, making the low end feel conversational. Bluhm sings in a cultivated baritone whose theatrical clarity recalls The Magnetic Fields, The Divine Comedy, Joseph Keckler, and Paul Jabara. Aid disappears before reaching those who need it. A senator is accused of surrendering principle to political money. A technology worker recognizes that the product supporting his livelihood may also aid surveillance and imprisonment. Then the view widens toward civilians leaving for work or school beneath falling bombs, and the singer confronts the accident of birthplace separating his safety from their deaths. His question, “what is our dark destiny allowing this to be?” carries the exhausted bewilderment of someone discovering how citizenship, employment, consumption, and conscience can become knotted together. “With Emotional Plea, I’d never written an overtly political protest song, but I felt I couldn’t ignore in my writing what’s happening around us, with ICE, with Gaza, with the complacency and lack of compassion,” says Bluhm. “I usually write slowly, but this came together quickly because I felt it so urgently. Mike Watt is one of the funkiest bass players I know, and I knew he’d be perfect for the song. I’m grateful he agreed. He sent his bass track back within 24 hours. The man works furiously.” The final verse turns toward Christianity, reducing doctrine to an almost childlike attempt at moral imitation. There is humour in the image, though Bluhm sings without a wink; behind it stands an accusation that compassion has become easier to profess than practice. Listen to Emotional Plea below and order the single here. Emotional Plea by Work Crush Work Crush uses no generative AI, and musician-illustrator Steve Teare drew the cover image of a child playing with a toy military plane. It is a severe emblem for a song in which distant violence enters domestic life. After the orchestral intimacy of Bluhm’s Out of the Nowhere Into the Here, this new project finds him facing outward, fastening political dread to bass, beat, and melody, asking how comfortably anyone can dance while the world is simultaneously burning and flooding. What times we live in. Follow Work Crush: Instagram Facebook Website Bandcamp Spotify The post “Senator, What Can You Do?” — New Wave Artist Work Crush Debuts With Political Protest Song “Emotional Plea” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._genre: post-punk / synth-pop / new wave / art pop
items._cn_summary: Work Crush的首支单曲《Emotional Plea》以迪斯科律动为骨架，合成器与Nile Rodgers式吉他点缀其间，Mike Watt的低音线兼具肌肉感与对话性。Stephen Bluhm的男中音清晰而带有剧场感，歌词聚焦美国政治困境——公民在私人生活与公共暴力之间的道德纠缠，从给参议员写信到刷到远方轰炸下的伤亡新闻，每一个细节都被还原为日常化的无力感。歌曲将政治绝望从口号转化为个体客厅里的具体场景，最后以近乎孩童式的基督教模仿收束，暗讽慈悲在当代更容易被宣称而非实践。制作上坚持不使用生成式AI，封面由插画家手绘完成，整体呈现出严肃的政治寓言气质，旋律优雅但态度锐利。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑围绕俄罗斯占领区约两万乌克兰儿童被强制迁移的真实事件展开，以传统与原创曲目交织的方式呈现沉重主题。乌克兰裔加拿大歌手Marichka联合加拿大与乌克兰两支音乐团队创作，以弓弦乐器、班杜拉琴、钢琴及双陶笛为主要编制，全女性阵容担任主唱与伴奏。专辑将传统仪式歌曲与当代叙事结合，如改编自民间送别歌的《Foreign Land》以温柔人声表达母女分离之痛，而《Rusalka》则以激烈方式呼唤自然精灵。专辑特别收录来自被毁城市马里乌波尔的被拐儿童之一、年仅十六岁的Lisa演奏的双陶笛独奏。音乐在克制与爆发之间切换，为战争罪行留下极具人文深度的声乐文献。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Embarking on an epic journey with a soundtrack playing in the background, that is the closest way to describe the experience of listening to Madness and Magic, the latest album by Arabs in Aspic. The opening track, "I Vow to Thee, My Screen," unfolds with an epic feel reminiscent of Rush, yet it also features symphonic touches and guitar-keyboard counterpoint characteristic of the most refined era of Genesis, featuring Steve Hackett and Tony Banks."Lullaby for Modern Kids, Part 1" creates a highly original acoustic atmosphere, aided by the percussion of the group's fifth member, Alessandro G. Elide. However, the organ and a choir lend an uncanny quality to the mood, as if stepping into a world imagined by Lewis Carroll, while a classical organ solo unfolds alongside a guitar part reminiscent of Pink Floyd. Masterfully employing psychedelic elements, the album addresses various types of addiction, to medication and new technologies, and how all of this distances us from reality; hence its detached, otherworldly quality, as if setting alienation itself to music. Perhaps we stop talking about it precisely when we are already deep within its grip."Lullaby for Modern Kids, Part 2" features delightful acoustic guitar work, and the echoes of early-era Gabriel return with striking force. The album offers a wealth of nuances and tonal colors, reflecting a range of modos, such as "High-Tech Parent," which evokes a Latin-tinged track by the Doobie Brothers. Fierce guitar work, accompanied by organ and percussion, creates moments of hypnotic rhythm, a soundscape the Norwegian quintet explores across both acoustic and electric dimensions.On "Madness and Magic," the interplay between Mellotron and synthesizers builds layers that pave the way for the album's centerpiece, "Heaven in Your Eye."Here, driven once again by synthesizers and Moog, the acoustic opening gives way to an ascent through inner and outer forests, a journey mirrored in the music and the highly expressive vocals. Dark, Black Sabbath-esque hard rock sections provide a stark contrast to Eastern-influenced melodies, where powerful riffs take command. The promise is ultimately fulfilled with sections of high dramatic tension, featuring distorted accelerations and organ followed by guitar, backed by Mellotron, like clouds accompanying lightning during a storm.
items._genre: heavy prog / psychedelic rock / symphonic prog
items._cn_summary: Arabs in Aspic的《Madness and Magic》以七十年代前卫摇滚为根基，融合交响化编曲与迷幻元素。开篇曲目兼具Rush的史诗气质与Genesis（Steve Hackett与Tony Banks时期）的键盘吉他对位，器乐编排层次丰富。专辑探讨现代人对药物与科技的依赖，以疏离超现实的音乐语言呈现成瘾主题。中段曲目以原声吉他与Gabriel时期人声回响构建童话式氛围，配合管风琴与合唱营造诡异色彩。标题曲中Mellotron与合成器交织，东方旋律与Black Sabbath式硬摇滚形成张力对比。挪威五人组在原声与电声维度间自由切换，Moog与合成器驱动的器乐段落兼具戏剧性与催眠节奏，是一部制作精致、致敬经典但突破有限的传统前卫摇滚作品。
